syllabus:
Unit 1: Foundations of Art, Aesthetics and Design Quality
Introduction to art and aesthetics. Definition of beauty, form and proportion.
Elements and principles of design: line, shape, colour, texture, balance, rhythm,
contrast and unity. The Design Quality Triangle and its three primary components,
namely aesthetics, function and usability. How the three components are balanced
against each other in a product, and how a change in one component affects the
others. Examples from everyday consumer products such as furniture, mobile phones
and televisions.

Unit 2: Art, Identity and Human Experience
Art as a medium of personal expression. How personal identity, memory, emotion and
lived experience are communicated through painting, sculpture, photography, music
and performance. Interpretation of an artwork by the viewer. Subjectivity of taste.
Why certain artworks remain valued across generations while artistic trends change.
Criteria used to judge artistic merit, originality and craftsmanship.

Unit 3: Art, Design and Society
Art as a mirror and as a transformative force in society. Art movements and social
change. Design and culture, tradition and modernity. Public art, craft traditions
and everyday objects. The role of art in questioning social norms, creating social
awareness and shaping public opinion. Ethics and responsibility of the designer
towards society and the environment.

blueprint.title: Art & Aesthetics in Design — Demonstration paper
blueprint.instructions:
Answer all questions.
Use neat labelled diagrams where necessary.
Support your answers with relevant examples.

sections.title: Section A — Art, aesthetics and society

paper_questions.text: Explain aesthetics, function and usability in the Design Quality Triangle. Use a familiar chair as an example to show how the three components interact.
paper_questions.answer: Aesthetics concerns the chair's visual and sensory character; function concerns support for sitting; usability concerns ease and comfort of use. A suitable example explains how a visual or structural change can affect the other components.
paper_questions.rationale: Prepared presentation example; not live AI output or a measured research result. Requires an explanation of three taught concepts and their relationship in an everyday product.

evidence.quote: aesthetics, function and usability.

paper_questions.notes: Presentation sample; review before adapting to a real assessment.

marking_guide.criterion: Explain their interaction using the chair example

paper_questions.text: Smartphone A has a visually striking interface with hidden controls. Smartphone B has plain styling and clearly labelled controls. Analyse two trade-offs between aesthetics and usability using the Design Quality Triangle.
paper_questions.answer: A justified answer compares the visual character and discoverability of the supplied interfaces, explains two possible trade-offs, and connects the comparison to function and usability. Either interface may be preferred when supported by a clear context.
paper_questions.rationale: Prepared presentation example; not live AI output or a measured research result. Requires reasoning about relationships and trade-offs, rather than merely naming the components.

evidence.quote: aesthetics, function and usability.

paper_questions.notes: Prepared review example: inspect the differing Bloom suggestions.

marking_guide.criterion: Connect the analysis to the Design Quality Triangle

suggestion.reason: Prepared presentation example; not live AI output or a measured research result. A staged disagreement for demonstrating professor control; not an actual model prediction.

paper_questions.text: A photograph shows an empty chair beside a family portrait in a dim room. Analyse how these visual choices could communicate memory and personal identity. Explain why two viewers might interpret the photograph differently.
paper_questions.answer: Possible interpretations link the empty chair to absence, the family portrait to shared identity, and the setting to memory or emotion. Alternative interpretations are acceptable when grounded in the described features and differences in viewers' experiences.
paper_questions.rationale: Prepared presentation example; not live AI output or a measured research result. Provides a complete visual scenario and asks for relationships between features, meaning and subjective interpretation.

evidence.quote: Art as a medium of personal expression.

paper_questions.notes: Presentation sample; review before adapting to a real assessment.

marking_guide.criterion: Analyse two features in relation to memory or identity

paper_questions.text: Two viewers disagree about a sculpture: one values technical craftsmanship while the other values originality. Evaluate both positions and give a justified judgment using criteria of artistic merit.
paper_questions.answer: A strong answer explains what each criterion contributes, recognises limitations of judging by only one criterion, and reaches a reasoned conclusion. No single preference is required.
paper_questions.rationale: Prepared presentation example; not live AI output or a measured research result. Requires a judgment supported by explicit criteria, while allowing more than one defensible conclusion.

evidence.quote: Criteria used to judge artistic merit, originality and craftsmanship.

paper_questions.notes: Presentation sample; review before adapting to a real assessment.

marking_guide.criterion: Evaluate craftsmanship and originality as criteria
Give a justified and balanced judgment

paper_questions.text: A campus proposes replacing a traditional craft display with a mass-produced installation. Evaluate one cultural and one environmental consequence, then recommend an approach that recognises the designer's responsibilities.
paper_questions.answer: Answers may consider continuity of craft traditions, representation, materials and resource use. Environmental effects should be explained as conditional possibilities because no life-cycle data are supplied. A recommendation must weigh both types of consequence.
paper_questions.rationale: Prepared presentation example; not live AI output or a measured research result. Connects a supplied social-design scenario to cultural context, ethics and environmental responsibility.

evidence.quote:
Ethics and responsibility of the designer
towards society and the environment.

paper_questions.notes: Presentation sample; review before adapting to a real assessment.

paper_questions.text: Propose a small public art installation that encourages waste segregation on a college campus. Describe its concept, materials and visitor interaction, and justify how it could create social awareness.
paper_questions.answer: One possible concept is an interactive installation using clearly separated reclaimed materials. Visitors place sample objects into labelled parts of the artwork. Any coherent, feasible proposal may be credited when its materials, interaction and awareness goal are justified.
paper_questions.rationale: Prepared presentation example; not live AI output or a measured research result. Asks for a new, bounded proposal with an explicit social purpose and a justified relationship between design and awareness.

evidence.quote: awareness and shaping public opinion.

paper_questions.notes: Presentation sample; review before adapting to a real assessment.
